units.la: ARtium bonarum non est tenuis usus & obscura utilitas in Ecclesia, curia, & Oeconomia. Sanè homines priuati, qui vel characteres literarum formare calamo, & expedire rationes mediocriter norunt, in metallica, mercatura & similibus negocijs magna dexteritate versantur. Nec minus ijdem juvantur anni cognitione ex diarijs, & mensuris, quam Astronomia & Geometria acceptâ debemus. Quanto autem, uberiores fructus copiosior doctrina præbet, in gravioribus studijs, religionis, & juris ciuilis? Quæ necessaria sunt, ne extinguatur notitia Dei inter homines, Sed ut seruetur Ecclesia & multi fiant hæredes vitæ æternæ, & custodiatur disciplina, plina, quæ est famæ, vitæ, & fortunarum tuenda-rum ratio. Qui disputationes Theologicas & forenses penitus introspiciunt, sæpe homines ingeniosissimos à methodo in grauissimis controuersijs deerrare, sæpe turpissima errata alia Grammatica & Dialectica deprehendunt, quæ tum Ecclesiæ, tum Reipublicæ nocent. Nam Ecclesia est Grammatica & Dialectica interpres sermonis diuini, & idem munus est sacerdotum justitiæ in foro, in professione sua. Quare omnibus ferè ætatibus homines sapientes, conseruandis rectis studijs magnos sumtus publicè & priuatim facuunt, & in ijsdem multum opera ponunt. Cum enim pauca vel à magnis artificibus, inuentis majorum & veterum adijci constet: & illa ἐγκαλλήψεις usum totius vitæ requirant, ut Socrates apud Platonem in Philebo docet, & his ipsis maxime opus sit, quæ tamen paruo negocio & paucis annis memoria complecti pueri possunt, ut ijsdem in omni vita utantur, quamuis alij multi, magno, diuturno & vario labore, tanquam cibum præmansum in os inferendum comparârunt: intelligunt homines mines cordati ac copiosi, integrum sibi non esse, committere, ut tanta solertia ac industria monumenta sua socordia & sordibus intercidant & pereant, ac necessarias utilitates humano generi præbere desinant. Secus qui faciunt, quid lucri quaso faciunt, nisi ut se indignos tantis bonis esse declarent, & Deo cuius munus illa sunt, ingratos, ac quia studiosos eorum aspernantur, res præclarissimas & carissimas, corpus vitam, existimationem, denique salutem omnem, hominibus nulla industria vel fide præditis credant & committant, qui vel nolunt, vel nequeunt præstare, quæ promittunt & necessitas requirunt. Et sic ulciscuntur ipsos sui mores tandem.
units.tr: The good arts have no slight or obscure use in the Church, the court and the household. Indeed, private persons who know how to form letters with a pen and to keep accounts reasonably well are highly skilled in mining, trade and similar business. Likewise, we owe no less to the knowledge of the year drawn from calendars and measures than to astronomy and geometry. But how much richer fruit does a fuller learning yield in the weightier studies of religion and civil law? These are necessary, not only so that the knowledge of God is not extinguished among men, but so that the Church is preserved, many become heirs of eternal life, and discipline is kept, which is the means of guarding one's reputation, life and property. Those who look closely into theological and legal disputations often find that men of the greatest talent go astray from the proper method in the gravest controversies, and often discover the most shameful errors in grammar and logic, which harm both the Church and the Republic. For the Church is the interpreter of the divine word by means of grammar and logic, and the same task belongs to the priests of justice in the courts, in their profession. Therefore, in almost every age, wise men have spent great sums, publicly and privately, on preserving sound studies, and have devoted much effort to them. For since it is agreed that few things have been added even by great craftsmen, to the discoveries of the elders and ancients, and since these things (the memorized notions, ἐγκαλλήψεις [ἐγκαλλήψεις]) require use throughout life, as Socrates teaches in Plato's Philebus, and since there is the greatest need for precisely those things which boys can nonetheless grasp in memory with little trouble and in a few years, so that they may use them all their lives, even though many others, with great, lasting and varied labour, have prepared them like food chewed beforehand to be put into the mouth; sensible and capable men understand that it is not right for them to allow such great skill and industry to perish and be lost through their own idleness and neglect, and to cease offering necessary benefits to the human race. Those who act otherwise, what gain do they seek, I ask, except to show themselves unworthy of such great goods, and ungrateful to God, whose gift they are? And because they despise those who study them, they entrust and commit the most precious and dear things, body, life, reputation and finally all safety, to men who lack diligence and good faith, who are unwilling or unable to perform what they promise and what necessity requires. And so, in the end, their own conduct takes its revenge on them.

units.la: Sed his omissis: Viri amplissimi, Domini & patroni colendi, quid velim potius aperiam. Æquis animis quaso, si vacat & molestum non est cognoscite. Cum nuper pro singulari vestro piorum & rectorum studiorum amore & cura, ad regenda juventutis vestra studia huc vocarer, fretus ope divina obtemperavi, & eam provinciam cepi. Initio autem, pro more, ad inserendas teneris animis honestas opiniones, de vita generibus diuinitus institutis, nonnulla commemoraui, eo ipso, quod in Epicureum λάδε βιώ- σας dixi. Quia vero benevole & candide judi-
units.tr: But setting these aside, most distinguished men, my honoured lords and patrons, I will rather explain what I wish. If you have leisure and it is not a burden, I ask you to hear me with an open mind. Since recently, through your singular love and care for the pious and upright studies, I was called here to direct the studies of your youth, I obeyed, trusting in divine help, and undertook that charge. At the start, however, as is customary, in order to instil honest opinions into tender minds, I related some things about the ways of life ordained by God, and I did so precisely by saying against the Epicurean maxim lathe biōsas [λάθε βιώσας]. Since, however, kindly and candid judg-

units.la: cantibus displicere non potest, quod meam volun-tatem notam esse cupio, & bonarum rerum celebrationem bonis omnibus gratam esse, & adolescentiam magno cū fructu suo repetitionem eorum, quæ semel audiuit, legere constat: declaraturus simul studium meum fauoris vestri, quem maximi facio & mihi etiam atq; etiam tuendum esse intelligo: amicorum hortatu hoc scriptum in lucem edere volui, & V. A. reue-renter offero. Acut pro eximia virtute vestra, benevolentia solita accipiatis, & me, una cum studijs meis vt hactenus benigne complecti & tueri pergatis, ac nūquam desinatis, magno-pere peto. Mihi nihil tam erit propositum, quam ut officijs publicis & priuatis, quibus me debere ac posse intelligam, vestris meritis sedu-lo respondeam. Oro æternum Deum, patrem Domini nostri Iesu Christi, vt inter cætera ve-stra Reipublica ornamenta multa & magna, quibus excellit, Dei beneficio, sacras & bonas liteliteras servet, vestram gubernationem & totam vitam optata prosperitate ornet, ut pietatis & virtutis praemia etiam in hac vita illustria percipiatis. Benè valete, Stadæ, Nonis Decembris anno Jesu Christi 1582.
units.tr: ing readers cannot be displeased that I wish my intention to be known, and it is agreed that the celebration of good things is pleasing to all good people, and that youth reads with great profit the repetition of what it has heard once; and wishing at the same time to declare my zeal for your favour, which I value most highly and which I understand must be guarded for me again and again, I have wished, at the urging of friends, to bring this writing into the light, and I reverently offer it to you, most honoured sirs. I earnestly ask that you receive it with your customary kindness, in view of your outstanding virtue, and that you continue, as hitherto, to embrace and protect me and my studies kindly, and never cease. Nothing will be more my purpose than to respond diligently, by your merits, to the public and private duties by which I understand I am bound and able to serve. I pray the eternal God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, that among the many great ornaments of your Republic, by which by God's blessing it excels, he preserve sacred and good letters, adorn your government and whole life with the wished-for prosperity, so that you may receive the rewards of piety and virtue, illustrious even in this life. Farewell. Stade, on the Nones of December, in the year of Jesus Christ 1582.
