units.la: ORATIO QVA VT COMMENDENTVR VITAE GENERA DIVINITVS INSTITVTA, REFELLITVR EPICVREUM λάθε βιώσας, quod vitam clandestinam praecipit & ab honestis ac necessariis humanae vitae officijs auocat.
units.tr: THE ORATION IN WHICH THE KINDS OF LIFE INSTITUTED BY GOD ARE COMMENDED AND EPICURUS' PRECEPT "LIVE HIDDEN" [λάθε βιώσας] IS REFUTED, because it teaches a concealed life and draws people away from the honourable and necessary duties of human life.

units.la: {D}Lacet disciplina, quod in hoc casu, qui haud dubie, ut Deo dicatus, ita eidem carus est, de bonis rebus nonnihil dicit initio, cui eius gubernatio demandatur. Nam voces eiusmodi bonio minis causa initia decent, & personare his aures puerorum, quamuis abest maturitas aetatis, non est inutile. Neq; talis oratio fere unquam intempestiua & ingrata hominibus moderatis esse & videri solet.
units.tr: It seems fitting for the school that in this case a man who is undoubtedly dedicated to God and dear to him should say something at the outset about good things, to whom its direction is entrusted. For words of this kind are appropriate at the beginning for the sake of good omens, and it is not useless for boys' ears to resound with them, even though they are not yet of mature age. Nor is such a speech usually unseasonable or unwelcome to moderate people, or seen as such.

units.la: Quare ut meo loco consuetudinem sequar, & simul vitae genera divinitus instituta, & omnes, qui in his versantur, me magnificare ostendam, refellere decrevi Epicureum λάθε βιώσας: Quod propter societatem generis humani, occultam & remotam ab oculis & usu aliorum vitam proponit ac suadet, & nescio in qua antra & lustra homines abducit & conjicit.
units.tr: Therefore, to follow the custom of my office, and at the same time to show that the kinds of life instituted by God and all who live in them deserve my praise, I have decided to refute Epicurus' precept "Live hidden" [λάθε βιώσας]. It proposes and urges a hidden life, withdrawn from the sight and use of others, and leads and drives people into I know not what caves and dens.

units.la: Odio dignum & detestandum esse illum stultae opinionis errorem omnes animadvertimus. Nam quia improbat & damnat vitae genera, quae admirando consilio & ingenti bonitate Deus instituit & sanxit, quaeq; & hic ornatissimus confessus & alij honesti homines amplectuntur & tenent, & in illum omnis boni fontem atq; autorem, & in hos humani generis antistites, contumeliosus est.
units.tr: We all notice that this error of foolish opinion deserves hatred and detestation. For it disapproves and condemns the kinds of life that God instituted and sanctioned with wonderful wisdom and great goodness, which this most distinguished confessor and other honest men embrace and hold to. In doing so it insults him, the fount and author of all good, and these leaders of mankind.

units.la: Virtus est dare, quod re ipsa debetur honori, Hostem esse atqʒ inimicum hominum, morumqʒ malorum: Contra defensorem hominum morumqʒ bonorum, secundum Lucilium. Quare, quamvis Reverendi & amplissimi viri, intelligens ac grave judicium vestrum vereor, praesertim ubi considero ingenij & doctrinae in me facultatem pertenuem, & quàm difficile sit, vt Xenophon gravissimus autor Socratem dixisse refert, aliquid conari & praestare citra errorem & accusationem, & ubi quid etiam verè & sine errore praestiteris, non incurrere in alicuius reprehensionem: tamen quoniam declaratis vestra praesentia, vestrae autoritati, fidei & prudentiae, munus nostrum destinatum scholis, quamlibet humile & spretum, commendatum & cordi esse: fretus insigni aequitate & humanitate vestra, qua etiam voluntatem solam boni consulere soletis, ubi vires desunt, ad rem Deo duce & comite accedo, & ardenter imploro ipsius opem, ac vt vestra benevolentia, more vestro meis conatibus praesidio sitis, studiosè oro.
units.tr: It is a virtue to give what is in fact owed to honour; to be the enemy and foe of men and of wicked morals; on the contrary, to be the defender of men and of good morals, according to Lucilius. Therefore, although I fear your distinguished and weighty judgement, most Reverend and Honoured Sirs, especially when I consider how slight my talent and learning are, and how difficult it is, as the weighty author Xenophon reports Socrates saying, to attempt and accomplish anything without error and blame, and even when you have done something truly and without error, not to incur someone's reproach: nevertheless, since by your presence you have declared that our task, assigned to the schools, however humble and despised, is commended to and dear to your authority, faith and prudence, I come to the matter, with God as leader and companion, trusting in your remarkable fairness and humanity, by which you are accustomed to accept the goodwill alone where ability is lacking. I fervently implore his help, and earnestly beg that, as is your way, you be a protection to my efforts with your kindness.

units.la: Asolitaria vita revocant, & ad colendam ac fouendam conjunctionem cum aliis hominibus nos hortantur: Alia nostra conditio, quam est & aliorum & inprimis animantium, quae in terrae visceribus degunt: illud Caelum: lux inde diffusa: Elementa: Corpora ex his condita & constituta: Nostra necessitas, Mutua generis nostri officia: Civitatum non nullarum, quas pro nostra re attingemus, conservatio: Artium principium ac ortus: Finis noster: Ea, quae justitiae munus à nobis exigit: Quae rationis & orationis facultas nobis imponit: Tum perpetua Dei praesentia in actionibus generi humano salutaribus, & insigniu atqʒ illustriu virorum res gestae: Deniqʒ auxilia & actiones Dei in sanctis, & multa ejusmodi alia: Qui jam stabit sententia contraria. Epicuri nitidis bene curata cute porcis, vt Poëtae verbis utare.
units.tr: These things call us back from a solitary life and urge us to cultivate and foster fellowship with other men: our other condition, which is shared with others and especially with the living creatures that dwell in the bowels of the earth; that heaven; the light diffused from it; the elements; the bodies made and constituted from these; our need; the mutual duties of our kind; the preservation of certain states, which we shall touch on as our subject requires; the origin and beginning of the arts; our end; what the duty of justice demands of us; what the faculty of reason and speech imposes on us; then God's constant presence in actions beneficial to the human race, and the deeds of distinguished and illustrious men; finally God's help and actions in the saints, and many things of this kind. Who will now uphold the contrary opinion? Epicurus' hogs, with their sleek and well-kept hides, as the poet says.

units.la: Animalia Φωλεύοντα, qualia sunt bestiae, quae insidias parant aut metuunt, intra sua cubilia & specus se receptant occultant. Hominem verò aliis benè velle & conferre, ab aliis expectare & accipere bona Deus & natura voluit. Itaq; non brutorum & ferarum more perpetuò meditari ac metuere dolos, & loco sibi cavere, latebras quaerere & abdere sese debet, qui ad κοινωνίαν natus est, ac ut Plato ait, est ζῷον Φύσει Πολιτικòν. Omnia, quae cœli templum ambit & tegit, ea instar mercium in amplissimo emporio, alia in aliis tabernis posita versantur. Itaq; elementa, aër, aqua, terra, & quae in cœlo & his domicilijs resident, stellae, plantae, animantia sub aspectum cadunt & videntur. Sunt enim ex eorum numero, quae sunt Aristoteli ὀρατὰ, ὧν ἐπι ὀψιϛ. Quare hominem eximere à statu rerum, quarum cognatione ac necessitudine detinetur, nefas est.
units.tr: Animals that hide themselves [Φωλεύοντα], such as beasts that lay snares or fear them, withdraw and conceal themselves within their lairs and caves. But God and nature willed that man should wish well to others and confer benefits, and should expect and receive good things from others. Therefore he who is born for fellowship [κοινωνίαν] ought not, after the manner of brutes and wild beasts, constantly to brood on deceits and fear them, guard his place, seek hiding-places, and hide himself away. As Plato says, man is a political animal by nature [ζῷον Φύσει Πολιτικόν]. Everything that the temple of heaven surrounds and covers lies in the manner of goods in a very large market, some placed in one shop, some in another. Thus the elements, air, water, earth, and what dwells in heaven and in these dwellings, the stars, plants and animals, fall under our sight and are seen. For they belong to the number of things that Aristotle calls visible [ὀρατὰ], of which sight is the perception [ὧν ἐπι ὀψιϛ]. Therefore it is wrong to remove man from the state of things with which he is bound by kinship and close connection.

units.la: Cum Deus natura opifex & origo melioris mundi, totam molem istam cum omni instrumento Elementorum, Corporum, Spirituum, ut disertissimus Tertullianus loquitur, verbo, quo jussit, ratione, qua disposuit, virtute, qua potuit è nihilo exprimeret in ornamentum majestatis suae, unde Graeci mundo nomen κόσμος accomodaverunt: ante omnia rudem & indigestam materiem creabat, quae Chaos est: De hoc cum manasset obscura fama ad homines, quorum majores tædio praesentium suorum bonorum, prima & verissima doctrina relicta, religiones novas fingere non dubitârant: materiam primam Deo coæternam commenti sunt: Et alia multa, quae primus liber Mosi habet, ista doctrina, vel majora vel non inferiora, ne levissima quidem suspicione attigerunt.
units.tr: Since God, the maker of nature and the origin of a better world, brought forth that whole mass with all its equipment of elements, bodies and spirits, as the most eloquent Tertullian puts it, out of nothing, by the word with which he commanded, by the reason with which he arranged, and by the power with which he could, to be the adornment of his majesty, whence the Greeks gave the world the name kosmos [κόσμος]; he first created the rude and undigested matter, which is Chaos. When an obscure report of this reached men, whose forefathers, weary of their present blessings, had not hesitated to invent new religions after abandoning the first and truest teaching, they devised the notion that primal matter was coeternal with God; and they touched, not even with the lightest suspicion, the many other things that the first book of Moses contains, which this teaching has either as great or no less importance.

units.la: Quod est inter argumenta certitudinis doctrinæ Christianæ non postremum. Qua de re nunc plus verborum facere nihil attinet. Absoluto primo hoc opere, proximum Deo fuit, ut lucem crearet, quae quoniam est ἐνεργεία, id est actu perspicua, ut Philosophi docent, & sese & alia corpora patefacit & ostendit. Hæc vel ipsa similiter sunt lucida, ut Sol ὀχημα πρωπρωτηγόνος Φωτὸς, secundum Basilium, & Luna remedium nocturnarum tenebrarum, & magistra omnium Φαινομένων, quæ in cælo observata sunt, & cætera astra: vel illustrari possunt, aut superficie tenus, ut quæ opaca & radijs lucis non sunt pervia, cujusmodi sunt, terra & plaraq; corpora è quatuor elementis constata: aut penitus, ut gemma, aër, & aqua, sine quorum adminiculo catera non cernuntur. Hæc singula & universa uno ore ac voce de hoc consentiunt: opera divina non latere & hominum conspectum effugere, sed aperta & visui exposita esse oportere. Eodem pertinet, quod Deus homines & animantia facultate & instrumentis videndi donavit, ut sese mutuò aspicerent & agnoscerent.
units.tr: This is not the least of the arguments for the certainty of Christian doctrine. There is no need to say more about this matter now. This first work finished, God's next act was to create light, which, since it is energeia [ἐνεργεία], that is, visible in act, as the philosophers teach, both reveals itself and shows other bodies. Some of these are similarly luminous, as the sun, the vehicle of primal light according to Basil, and the moon, the remedy of nocturnal darkness and the teacher of all the appearances observed in heaven, and the other stars; or they may be illumined on the surface only, like things that are opaque and not permeable to rays of light, such as earth and many bodies made of the four elements; or entirely, like a gem, air and water, without whose aid other things are not discerned. All these singly and together agree in one voice that the works of God ought not to lie hidden or escape human sight, but to be open and exposed to view. To the same end belongs the fact that God gave men and animals the faculty and instruments of sight, so that they might look upon and recognise one another.

units.la: Quamobrem, qui ex hominum societate emigrandum, & discedendum sibi in solitudinem & ibi delitescendum existimat, na ille insigni quadam nota & ignominia afficere & condemnare videtur, quæ sagacissimo consilio solertia divinæ constituta sunt. Et totam rerum naturam & homines inprimis mutuo & arctissimo fœdere obstrictos esse sibi Deus voluit. Itaq; alias naturas aliis, & quidem hominem plus omnibus indigere voluit à natali suo, quo hanc lucem aspicere incipit, usq; ad extremum halitum, quo lucis usura privatur. Elementis opus est cælo & stellis, à quibus foveantur & colorem quendam accipiant. Est enim lux secundum Philosophum color quidam, sine quo aer & aqua sunt informia & obscura, & alia colorum genera dignosci non possunt. Cælum verò arduum illud & amplissimum culmen inferioribus corporibus apta serie contiguis incumbit, & his quasi fultum sustinetur, donec terra insistentia in hoc centro desinant & finiantur. Idem tamen cælum, Elementa & quæ his constant, appetit & requirit magis, ut suas in hac opes transfundat. Est enim divina quadam bonitate praditum, ac molestum ipsi futurum erat, si non essent alia naturaturæ, in quas divitias exoneraret. Sed de his vberius & subtilius disserunt, qui singulari studio scrutantur & persequuntur eam, quam Cicero vocat, naturæ obscuritatem. Sequitur aër mobilis, circundans & ventilans aquas, ne si staent immotæ vitium capiant & putrescant, ad quam rem vapores & exhalationes adferunt adjumenta. Cæli vero tenuitate & calore temperatus aër, vitalem & salutarem Spiritum dat omni generi animantium. Infra aërem situs est Oceanus magnus, qui multas in terram venas spargit & aquam diffusam & distributam quasi per canales, ostijs vel manifestis vel occultis, rursus ad se admittit, & sinu suo excipit, tum terra affluit & interfluit, ut ex utrisq; globus convexus fiat, cujus unum est centrum, & non duplex, aliud gravitatis, aliud magnitudinis, ut nonnulli tradiderunt. His Elementis meteora egent, meteoris ac reliquis superioribus corporibus plantæ, plantis unà cum suis adminiculis animantia, Omnibus ijs conjunctim & omnium maximè Deo, ac se inter se homines.
units.tr: Therefore, whoever thinks that he must emigrate from human society, withdraw into solitude and hide himself there, seems to brand and condemn himself with a certain distinct mark and disgrace, for these things were established by divine providence with the most sagacious plan. God willed that the whole of nature, and man above all, should be bound together by a mutual and very close bond. Thus he willed that different natures should need different things, and man more than all others, from his birth, when he first begins to see this light, to his last breath, when the use of light is taken from him. He needs the elements, heaven and the stars, by which he is cherished and receives a certain colour; for light, according to the Philosopher, is a kind of colour, without which air and water are formless and dark, and the other kinds of colour cannot be distinguished. Heaven, that lofty and very large canopy, rests on the lower bodies in a fitting, continuous series, and is held up as if supported by them, until the earth, on which they stand, ends and terminates at this centre. Yet heaven itself, the elements and what they consist of, crave and seek still more to pour out their riches into this world; for heaven is endowed with a certain divine goodness, and it would have been troublesome for it if there were no other natures into which it might unload its riches. But these matters are discussed more fully and subtly by those who study and pursue with special zeal that obscurity of nature which Cicero calls so. Next comes the mobile air, which surrounds and stirs the waters, lest, if they stood still, they should contract corruption and rot; for this purpose vapours and exhalations provide help. And air, tempered by the thinness and warmth of heaven, gives a vital and healthful spirit to every kind of living creature. Beneath the air lies the great Ocean, which spreads many veins into the earth and, as if through channels with openings either visible or hidden, takes back again the water that has been diffused and distributed, and receives it in its bosom; then the earth flows around and through it, so that from both a convex globe is made, of which there is one centre and not two, one of heaviness and another of magnitude, as some have taught. Meteors need these elements; plants need the meteors and the other higher bodies; animals need the plants along with their aids; and all of these together need God most of all; and men need one another.

units.la: Quare verbis dici satis non potest, quanta Dei sapientia variæ artes & vitæ genera instituta & in societatem hominum introducta sint, in quibus homines multiplicibus beneficijs ac officijs mutuas inter se operas tradant ac certent. Sed Μισάνθρωπος aliquis, qui usum consuetudinis suæ omnem aliis negat & subtrahit, is praeterquam quod sanctioni divinæ refragatur, non tantum alios, sed etiam seipsum in desidia negligat, imo sibi maximum damnum det necesse est. Nam qui se in cavea quapiam perpetuò concludit & alios à se excludit, quid ab aliis boni capiat? quid ijsdem conferat? denique quid agat? Quanto praestantiora insecta & vermes sunt? Certè formicæ melius in se & suum genus consulunt, quæ memores hyemis venturæ, noctu Luna plena, grana sibi & suis convehunt hunt ac reponunt, nihil neq; laboris molestiam, neq; suam imbecillitatem, neq; pondus, quod granis, feré ipsorum corpusculis majus est, veritæ. Apes autem, non tantum sui, sed etiam hominum rationem habere videntur, suo cum commodo illorum commoda comparantes. Nam libantes omnia in saltibus floridis mella construunt. Quæ non modo ipsis pabulo sunt, sed præterquam quod gustatum hominis, nectaris instar mirifice capiunt sua dulcedine, etiam in cibis & salutaribus remedijs vsum maximum habent. Sui verò nullam, hominum omnem curam agere videntur horridæ erucæ, quas bombyces vocamus, qui quasi ex latente stamine in suis corpusculis, subtilissima & preciosissima fila educunt & gignunt, quibus & uti ipsæ nesciunt, & homines se amiciunt & ornant,
units.tr: Therefore it cannot be said in words how greatly God's wisdom has established the various arts and ways of life and introduced them into human society, in which people trade mutual labours with one another and vie in offering manifold benefits and services. But a misanthrope, who denies others the use of his company and withdraws it from them, not only opposes the divine ordinance but necessarily neglects not only others but himself in idleness, and indeed does himself the greatest harm. For he who shuts himself up perpetually in some cage and shuts others out, what good does he get from others? What does he contribute to them? In short, what does he do? How much better are insects and worms! Surely ants look after themselves and their kind more wisely, for they, mindful of the coming winter, carry and store grain for themselves and their own under the full moon at night, shrinking from no toil, no weakness, and no burden, which is nearly greater than their own little bodies. Bees seem to have regard not only for themselves but also for the interests of humans, balancing their own advantage with ours. For sipping from everything in flowery meadows, they build honey, which is not only food for themselves but, besides being tasted by humans, is wonderfully pleasant like nectar and has very great use in foods and wholesome remedies. The horrid caterpillars we call silkworms, on the other hand, seem to take no thought for themselves but care for humans: they draw out and produce from their own little bodies, as from a hidden thread, the finest and most precious threads, which they themselves do not know how to use, and with which humans clothe and adorn themselves.

units.la: Similia alia in natura multa sunt. Quæ homines à natura bene informati admirantur, & eò magis aliis vel ope vel arte vel opera, prodesse studeant. Nihil horum præstant, qui lucem fugiunt & ignoti sunt.
units.tr: Many other similar things are found in nature. Men well instructed by nature admire these, and the more they strive to benefit others by help, skill or work. Those who flee the light and remain unknown achieve none of these things.

units.la: Qualis quaso ovium patris custos fuit Epimenides septem decades annorum & etiam aliquanto amplius latens, seu vigilans seu dormiens in speláo?
units.tr: What sort of guardian of sheep, I ask, was Epimenides, who lay hidden in a cave, whether awake or asleep, for fifty-seven years and even somewhat longer?

units.la: Incustoditi pylios memorantur in agros processisse boves secundum Metamorphosin. Quis aravit, sementum fecit, putavit arbores & vites, fodit & repastinavit vineas in occulto dolio, in quo ne quidem figulinam quisquam exercet juxta vetus verbum? Nonne videmus institores & opifices, apud quos venales sunt cibi, medicamenta, vestes, arma & id genus alia, occupare officinas & demissis valuis sedere in apertis tabernis?
units.tr: We are told that unattended oxen went out into the fields of Pylos, according to the Metamorphosis. Who ploughed, sowed, pruned trees and vines, and dug and trenched vineyards in a hidden jar, in which, as the old saying goes, no one even works as a potter? Do we not see shopkeepers and craftsmen, at whose places food, medicines, clothing, weapons and other such things are for sale, occupying their workshops and sitting in open shops with their doors let down?

units.la: Qui metalla effodiunt, lapides excidunt è terra, tecta construunt ad vim frigoris pellendam & calorum molestias sedandas: Qui condunt aquæ ductus, portus, moles opponunt fluctibus, pharmaca propinant ægrotis: Qui venantur, Qui docent, disputant, scribunt, à vitijs revocant, ad virtutem excitant, defendunt bonos, compescunt malos, nihil horum clàm vel furtim faciunt, aut vt nesciantur, & ignobiles atq; obscuri sint. Quis vllam vnquam artem perdidicit clausus in tenebroso ergastulo, vel continens se intra privatos parietes, neq; magistros ad se intromittens vel ad eos egrediens? Nulla enim ars sine literis, sine magistro & interprete, & pessimus sibi quisq; magister est. Quis in turpitudinis casibus implicitus haerens, inde expeditus ad virtutis castra retractus est ac redit, meliora ac saniora scientibus ac monentibus incognitus, ab ijsq; non interpellatus.
units.tr: Those who dig up metals, quarry stone from the earth, build houses to ward off the force of cold and to relieve the discomforts of heat; those who dig aqueducts and harbours, set up dams against the waves, and give medicines to the sick; those who hunt; those who teach, dispute, write, call people back from vices, rouse them to virtue, defend the good and restrain the wicked, do none of these things secretly or by stealth, or so that they may go unknown and remain obscure and undistinguished. Who ever learned any art while shut up in a dark prison, or while confining himself within private walls, admitting no teachers to himself and going out to none? For no art exists without letters, without a teacher and interpreter, and the worst teacher is each man to himself. Who, entangled in the mire of shameful circumstances, has been drawn back and returned to the camp of virtue unless he was known to those who knew better and wiser things and advised him, and was not reproached by them?

units.la: Alitur vitium, vivitq; tegendo.
units.tr: Vice is nourished, and lives by being hidden.

units.la: Dum medicas adhibere manus ad vulnera pastor Abstinet, & meliora Deus sedet omnia poscens:
units.tr: While the shepherd refrains from applying healing hands to the wounds, and God sits demanding all better things

units.la: ait Maro
units.tr: says Maro

units.la: Nonnullarum vrbium & Rerumpublicarum conserva-tionem spectemus. Si Romanis ignotus fuisset Camillus, nunquid ab ipso defensa & protecta fuisset vrbs adversus Gallos Senones? Nūquid victus esset exercitus Xerxis numerosissimus, qui bibens exhauriebat magna flumina, & servatæ à Themisto cle Athenæ fuissent, Themistocle nunquā à suis civibus audito & viso? Epaminondas ad quadragesimum annum aetatis usq; obscurus, nihil rebus Thebanis commodavit. Postea imperator factus Pelopidam à Thessalis captum liberavit, Rempublicam percuntem servavit, & servitutem à cervicibus Graciæ depulit, ac ad Mantineam pulcram pro patria per vulnera mortem petijt, victis hostibus Spartanis, quos nihil tale metuentes subito fuerat adortus. Plato ille divinus, vt vocatur à multis, si omnes homines latuisset inclusus atq; abditus in locis solis, quì suo consilio Dioni autor fuisset in asserenda in libertatem Sicilia? Sed de his hactenus. Ad qualibet eximia opera multi opeti operas omnibus temporibus conferunt, de quibus singulis dicere nunc nimis longum esset: saltem quomodo ars medica orta sit videamus. Nam ex hac de similibus idem intelligitur.
units.tr: Let us consider the preservation of some cities and commonwealths. If Camillus had been unknown to the Romans, would the city have been defended and protected by him against the Senones of Gaul? Would the most numerous army of Xerxes, which drank up great rivers, have been defeated, and would Athens have been saved by Themistocles, if Themistocles had never been heard and seen by his fellow citizens? Epaminondas, obscure until his fortieth year of life, lent nothing to Theban affairs. Afterwards, made commander, he freed Pelopidas, who had been captured by the Thessalians, saved the perishing commonwealth, drove slavery from the necks of Greece, and sought death for his country by wounds at beautiful Mantinea, the Spartan enemies having been defeated, whom he had suddenly attacked while they feared nothing of the kind. That divine Plato, as he is called by many, if he had lain hidden and shut away in lonely places, who would have been the adviser to Dion in asserting the liberty of Sicily? But enough of these things for now. Many people in every age contribute their labours to all kinds of excellent works, of which it would now be too long to speak individually; at least let us see how the medical art arose, for from this the same may be understood concerning similar things.

units.la: Proditum est memoriae ac literis à Plutarcho, apud Priscos, ægrotos sub dio fuisse positos, & unumquemque, qui aliquid salutifera medicina explorate perceptum cognitumque haberet, id admonuisse ægroto. Ita ars medica singularibus experimentis observatis & annotatis Coepit, & paulatim creuit, donec ordine digestum & constitutum extitit corpus eius, quod habemus, quod Φαρμακευτικὴν attinet. Convertamus animos & cogitationes ad ea, quae omnibus hominibus communia sunt. Non Deus ad iners ocium, sed ad solers negocium genus humanum condidit, ac quidem, ut inter cetera animalia bonus esset ac deprehenderetur homo, voluit. At bonitas, justitia & aequitate constat, quae in rationis & orationis expertes feras non cadit. Illam autem suam conditionem praestantissimam, homo quî tuebitur in desertissima solitudine? Ibi enim neque res familiaris neque publica esse potest. Quis ergo honestissimus & saluberrimis actionibus ibidem locus erit? in quibus omnis laus virtutis est.
units.tr: It has been handed down to memory and writing by Plutarch that among the ancients the sick were laid out in the open air, and that whoever had explored and learned something of a healing remedy reliably would advise the sick person. Thus the medical art began, with particular experiences being observed and recorded, and gradually grew, until that body of knowledge which we have, so far as it concerns pharmacy, was arranged in order and established. Let us turn our minds and thoughts to those things which are common to all men. God did not found the human race for idle leisure but for diligent business, and indeed he willed that man should be good and be recognised as good among the other animals. But goodness consists in righteousness, justice and equity, which do not fall to beasts that lack reason and speech. How can a man preserve that most excellent condition of his in the most deserted solitude? For there can be neither private nor public affairs there. What place, then, will there be for the most honourable and wholesome actions there, in which all the praise of virtue lies?

units.la: Quid justitia à nobis exigat, reputemus. Quot publicè & privatim beneficia homines ab hominibus percipiunt? Nam nisi varia & assidua aliorum ope omnes subleventur, vix paucos in dies spiritum singuli ducent, ac usura lucis huius fruentur. At beneficiarij, ut veteri verbo utar, imitari agros fertiles debent, qui ferè plus reddunt, quàm acceperunt. Solitarius autem, omnium meritorum turpissimè oblivisci tur. Imo cum ratio & oratio bona nobilissima data sint hominibus, ut docendo, discendo, communicando, disceptando & judicando illos inter se coeant, & conjungat naturali quadam societate quid praeter humani oris figuram & nomen sibi relinquit, qui quasi mutus tus & brutus se necessaria hominum consuetudine abdicat?
units.tr: Let us consider what justice demands of us. How many benefits do men receive from men, both publicly and privately? For unless everyone is sustained by the varied and constant help of others, scarcely a few individuals would draw breath each day and enjoy the use of this light. But beneficiaries, to use the old saying, ought to imitate fertile fields, which generally yield more than they received. The solitary man, however, most basely forgets all such services. Indeed, since reason and good speech have been given to men as the noblest gifts, so that by teaching, learning, sharing, disputing and judging they may come together and be joined in a certain natural society, what is left of him beyond the shape and name of a human face, who, like a dumb and brutish creature, withdraws himself from the necessary companionship of men?

units.la: Nonne homines magis inopes & vagi, & infeliciores belluarum gregibus essent, si plærique sibi unicè vivendum & consulendum esse censerent? Sed ferè semper integer numerus & justa copia est eorum, qui rebus humanis emolumento & subsidio esse student. Est enim conjunctio hominum in pagis, urbibus, regionibus, regnis, in quibus vigent, pecuaria, agricultura, contractus, artes, curatio morborum, juris æqua descriptio, doctrinæ cœlestis explicatio, pax, disciplina, conjugia, œconomiæ, judicia, pœnæ, magistratus, Res publicæ, Ecclesiæ, & variÿ in his singulis personarum gradus & discrimina, & sociatae humanæ vincula. Sed ut in mœnibus turres ac in orbe terrarum montes, sic in genere humano divinitus heroum genus eminet atq; excellit, & ad alios inferiores & tenuiores juvandos tutandos, & conservandos arcano & admirabili naturæ impetu rapitur & fertur, cui non somnus, non ludus, non jocus, non spectacula, non vinum, denique nullæ voluptatum illecebræ potiores sunt vigiliis, curis, laboribus, periculis, quæ pro aliorum tranquillitate, pudore, libertate & similibus bonis sustinenda sunt. Nam virtutum præstantia à Deo quidem, sed non sine ingenti animi & corporis contentione datur, ut de Æacidis Polybius Hesiodi versum recitat: ἀιανιδ' αι πολέμῳ κεχαρήστερ ἠέγε δαιτὶ, id est, Æacidæ bello magis gavisi sunt quàm convivio.
units.tr: Would not men be more needy, wandering and unhappier than herds of beasts, if most of them thought that they should live and look after themselves alone? But there is almost always a whole number and a fair supply of those who strive to be of profit and help to human affairs. For men are joined together in villages, cities, regions and kingdoms, in which there flourish herding, agriculture, contracts, arts, the cure of diseases, the just ordering of law, the explanation of heavenly doctrine, peace, discipline, marriages, households, judgments, punishments, magistrates, commonwealths, churches, and the various grades and distinctions of persons in each of these, and the bonds of human society. But just as towers rise above walls and mountains above the globe, so among mankind a race of heroes stands out and excels by divine gift, and is carried and driven by a hidden and wondrous impulse of nature to help, protect and preserve others who are lower and humbler. For them neither sleep, nor play, nor jest, nor spectacles, nor wine, in short no allurements of pleasure, are more attractive than vigils, cares, labours and dangers, which must be endured for the tranquillity, honour, liberty and similar goods of others. For the excellence of virtues is given by God, indeed, but not without great striving of mind and body, as Polybius recites of the Aeacids a verse of Hesiod: "The Aeacids rejoiced more in war than in feasting", that is, the Aeacids took more delight in war than in a banquet.

units.la: Insomniam, quam multis violentia & crudelitas conciliat, Themistoclii trophæa Miltiadis in Marathone posita afferebant. Quare noctu in publico oberrabat, & quærentibus causam, non diffitebatur. Nam infelix est gubernator, tota quicunq; quiescere nocte sustinet, & somnos vel alias voluptates tates præmia magna vocat, ut Sardanapalus pingens genas fucis, & muliebri stola in gynecais sedens, omissa imperij cura, vel Antonius agitans convivia, & vivens Bachanalia cum sua Cleopatra, securus belli, quo petitur & opprimitur ab Augusto.
units.tr: Insomnia, which violence and cruelty bring to many, was brought on Themistocles by the trophies of Miltiades set up at Marathon. So he wandered about in public at night, and when people asked why, he did not deny it. For whoever is willing to rest through the whole night is a wretched pilot. Those who call sleep and other pleasures great rewards are like Sardanapalus, painting his cheeks with cosmetics and sitting among women in a woman's robe, having dropped all concern for empire, or like Antony, who held banquets and lived out Bacchanalian revels with his Cleopatra, careless of the war by which he was pursued and crushed by Augustus.

units.la: Sicut avis, quæ pro pullis implumibus ipsa Evolat, & pastum miseris parat, haud secus ipse Pro Danais mala multa ferens, quot sape peregi Pervigiles noctes? quot luces Marte cruentas? Assiduo dum bella gero, dum prælior ipsis Progv viris & conjugibus Danaumq; salute.
units.tr: Like a bird that flies out for its unfledged chicks and brings them food, so I, bearing many evils for the Danaans, how often have I spent sleepless nights? How many days bloody with war have I endured? While I wage war without end, while I fight for the men and wives of the Danaans and for their safety.

units.la: Inquit Achilles Iliados nono: Non, ut Perseus, posterioris Philippi Macedonis filius, qui ante postremum prælium, quo captus est à Paulo Æmylio, muliercularum more discurrebat ad fana Deorum, & ignavis precibus petebat victoriam: Sic & Iosue, quanquam e cælo se ostendit ipsi quispiam, qui se ducè esse exercitus dicit, ociosus tamen non est neq; vel diffidentia, ac timiditate, vel securitate nihil agit: Sed ardenter orans, justam diligentiam adhibet, distribuit copias, collocat in insidiys, dimicat fortiter cum hoste, & victor Deo juvante triumphat.
units.tr: Achilles, in the ninth book of the Iliad, says: Not like Perseus, son of the later Philip of Macedon, who before the final battle, in which he was captured by Aemilius Paulus, ran about like a silly woman to the temples of the gods and with cowardly prayers begged for victory. So too Joshua, although someone appeared to him from heaven saying that he was the leader of the army, was nonetheless not idle. He did not do nothing out of distrust and timidity, nor out of complacency. Instead, praying fervently, he applied due diligence, distributed his forces, posted an ambush, fought bravely with the enemy, and triumphed as victor with God's help.

units.la: Agendo enim, ut vetus verbum ait, res Romana creuit, & πόνε χωρὶς ἡδὺν ἐντυχεῖα, ut Sophocles in Electra dicit, & Plutarchus in vita Pauli Æmylij: Non fas est, non jaculantem, ferire scopum, aut non stantem in acie vincere, aut nihil agentem esse felicem, aut ignavum esse beatum. Itaq; non aqua, non venti, non ignis, sed fulminis instar, ut de Hercule Pindarus Lyricorum princeps dicit, Heroici viri occasiones rerum gerendarum arripiunt & usurpant. Ac celeritate se hostes antevertisse, patientia amicos vicisse, Iulius Cæsar, haud scio an magis humaniter, quam sapienter, crebrò ducebat. Exempla autem similia multa, annalium commentarij suppeditant. Credimus dimús ne, si vita arcana & obscura, illa aperta & omnibus expósita esset potior, aut illos, quos diximus, acrem & vehementem ingenÿ incitationem ad res magnas habituros fuisse, aut eosdem naturæ semina secuturos? Donec Deus genus humanum conseruatum vult, singulatibus animi, corporis & fortunæ bonis semper aliquos homines præcæteris instruit, quæ gradus hominum in vita utiles faciunt. Illa vero nullius momēt & frustra concessa viderentur, si non in priuatis & publicis negocÿs apparerent & conspicerentur. At frustra & sine causa quid facere Deo non dignum est, quod abhorret etiam ab hominis constantia. Architectus nauem extructam, malo, remis, velis instructam, permittit nautis. Hi vero, quando cum pede & clauo, artis ratione eam gubernare nequeunt, relinquunt ventis. Deus autem non modo valetudine, robore corporis, magnitudine animi, eloquentia, acie & perspicacitate mentis, & similibus dotibus plurimis & maximis, afficit & cumulat homines, Sed ÿsdem etiam semper adest, & facit ut quæ agunt, secunda sint, suo arbitrio, ad agnitionem sui hoc pacto ipsos inuitans & ducens. Quod etiam naturæ luce viderunt, quos gentiles vocamus, ut Ausonÿ eloquÿ Tullius ipse pater, in Oratione pro Rabirio fatetur: Dei ope & auxilio, multò magis Rempubl: Romanam, quàm consilio administrari & regi. Et hinc sunt γνῶμαι ἀποφαντικαὶ καὶ παραινετικαὶ de irritis conatibus humanis & infelicitate omnium actionum, in quibus Deus postremas partes fert, apud Pindarum & alios: Ἐα πόλεμον, ἐα μαχλῶ Χωρὶς Θεῦ. Χωρὶς Θεῦ ἀδὲν εὐτυχεῖ βροτοῖς Mitte bellum, mitte prælium sine Deo, Sine Deo nihil est hominibus prosperum.
units.tr: For by acting, as the old saying goes, the Roman state grew, and "toil apart from pleasure is fortunate" [πόνος χωρὶς ἡδονῆς ἐντυχεῖν], as Sophocles says in the Electra, and as Plutarch says in the life of Aemilius Paulus. It is not right that one who does not throw should hit the mark, nor that one who does not stand in the battle line should win, nor that one who does nothing should be happy, nor that the idle should be blessed. So it is not water, nor winds, nor fire, but like a thunderbolt, as Pindar, prince of the lyric poets, says of Hercules, that heroic men seize and make use of the opportunities for doing great things. Julius Caesar often said that he had outstripped his enemies by speed and conquered his friends by patience, perhaps more humanely than wisely, I am not sure which. Many similar examples are supplied by the records of history. Do we really think that if a hidden and obscure life were preferred to one open and exposed to all, those men we have mentioned would have had a keen and vehement spur to great deeds, or would have followed the seeds of their nature? As long as God wills the human race to be preserved, he always equips some men above others with separate gifts of mind, body and fortune, which make these ranks of men useful in life. Yet those gifts would seem of no account and granted in vain if they did not appear and show themselves in private and public affairs. But what God would not do in vain and without cause, he abhors even in human constancy. An architect entrusts a built ship, fitted with mast, oars and sails, to sailors. But when they cannot steer it with tiller and helm by the rules of their craft, they abandon it to the winds. God, however, not only endows and heaps men with health, bodily strength, greatness of spirit, eloquence, keenness and insight of mind, and many other great gifts, but is also always present with them and makes what they do succeed, by his own will, thereby inviting and leading them to the knowledge of himself. Those whom we call Gentiles saw this even by the light of nature, as Tully himself, father of Ausonian eloquence, confesses in his speech for Rabirius: the Roman commonwealth is governed and ruled much more by the power and help of God than by human counsel. Hence come the Greek maxims, both declaratory and admonitory, about the futile efforts of men and the unhappiness of all human actions, in which God takes the last place, found in Pindar and others: "Leave war, leave battle without God. Without God nothing turns out well for mortals" [Ἔα πόλεμον, ἔα μαχλῶ χωρὶς θεοῦ. Χωρὶς θεοῦ οὐδὲν εὐτυχεῖ βροτοῖς].

units.la: Certè Aiax Telamonius, qui opem diuinam superbè fastidiestidiebat, & ad inertes relegabat, suæ strenuitatis confidentia, temeritatis justas gravesq; pœnas persoluit, quod furore percitus in arietem primum ut Vlyssem, deinde in greges tanquam in Vlyssis socios ac milites, tandem in seipsum sauijt, & adigens gladium in sua viscera, mortem sibi consciuit. Et Timotheus filius Cononis, qui sumtu suo muros Athenarum refecit, ad tibiarum cantum a Lysandro euersos (minimè Timotheus) patriæ utilis esse desijt, postquam, in concionem veniens, victus hostibus gloriatus est, hæc ego feci, non fortuna.
units.tr: Certainly Ajax, son of Telamon, who proudly scorned divine help and dismissed it to the idle, paid the just and heavy penalty for his rashness, trusting in his own strength. Driven by madness, he first raged against a ram as if it were Ulysses, then against the flocks as if they were Ulysses' companions and soldiers, and at last against himself: driving the sword into his own vitals, he brought death upon himself. And Timotheus, son of Conon, who at his own expense rebuilt the walls of Athens, which had been overthrown to the sound of flutes by Lysander (by no means by Timotheus), ceased to be useful to his country. He came before the assembly, defeated by his enemies, and boasted: "I did these things, not fortune."

units.la: Quod nimis insolens ac tumens dixit, ut expueret ex animo molestiam conceptam ex injuria, ut ipsi videbatur, non musi tanda, quæ beneficium verius, quàm injuria erat. Nam admonitus fuerat modestiæ tabula picta, in qua jnerat pictura hæc: Mollibus stratis jnuolutus Timotheus, stertebat ac dormiebat in vtramuis aurem. Interim fortuna peruigil tendiculas & laqueos ponebat, & irretiebat insulas ac urbes, ut expergefactus Timotheus eas haberet, &sic sines Atticos non proferre non posset. Ideo Nestor Homericus Palladem Telemacho poculum dare libandum jubet, ratiocinans eum Deo libenter studioseq; preces adhibere, quoniam omnibus hominibus ipso sit opus. Aratus autem Deum ubiq; nobis opportune præsentem, ut necessitas nostra postulat, & similiter ipso nos indigere statuens, omnes actiones cum ipsius celebratione & invocatione suscipiendas esse monet. At Zaleucus, Rex Locrensium, suos ciues non solum actione, Sed proposito, quod est constans & perpetua voluntas, bonos esse jussit, addens illustrem & grauissimam rationem: Quod Deus non honoretur sumtu, Sed virtute. Et Plato in Epinomide & Alcibiade damnat eorum delirationem, qui Deum præmiis & gestibus compositis, ut faneratorem, vel hominem qui se adulari sinit cupit, opinantur delectari. Vnde & illud Aristotelis ad Theo- decten manasse videtur, ἐκ εἰκὸς θεὸν χαίρειν τῶ σ δαπάναις τῶν θυομένων, ἀλλὰ τοῖς εὐσεβίαις ἴῶν θυοῦσιν. In quam senten- tiam, quasi verbum verbo exprimens Poëta Sulmonensis, de illis Aristoteleis, cecinit tam pie, quam eleganter: Non boue mactato caelestia numina gaudent, Sed quae praestanda est & sine teste fide.
units.tr: He spoke too insolently and proudly, as if to spit out of his mind the annoyance conceived from an injury, as it seemed to him, though it was not an injury but rather a benefit. For he had been warned by a painted tablet of modesty, on which was this picture: Timotheus, wrapped in soft coverlets, lay snoring and sleeping on either ear. Meanwhile Fortune, ever watchful, set her snares and nets and entangled islands and cities, so that Timotheus, when roused, would have them, and thus could not fail to extend the borders of Attica. So Homer's Nestor bids Telemachus give Pallas a cup for libation, reasoning that he gladly and zealously offers prayers to God, since all men have need of him. Aratus, holding that God is always present to us, opportunely as our need requires, and that we likewise need him, advises that all actions be undertaken with his praise and invocation. Zaleucus, king of the Locrians, ordered his citizens to be good not only in action but in purpose, which is a constant and perpetual will, adding an illustrious and weighty reason: that God is honoured not by expense but by virtue. Plato, in the Epinomis and the Alcibiades, condemns the folly of those who think God delights in gifts and elaborate gestures, as a moneylender does, or as a man does who lets himself be flattered. Whence also that saying of Aristotle to Theodectes seems to have flowed: "It is not likely that God rejoices in the expense of the victims that are sacrificed, but in the piety of those who sacrifice" [οὐκ εἰκὸς θεὸν χαίρειν ταῖς δαπάναις τῶν θυομένων, ἀλλὰ ταῖς εὐσεβείαις τῶν θυόντων]. Expressing this same sentiment almost word for word, the poet of Sulmo sang of these Aristotelian ideas, as piously as elegantly: "Not with a slaughtered ox do the heavenly powers rejoice, but with faith that is to be kept and needs no witness."

units.la: Achilles vero his omnibus adjecit apud Homerum: Χρὴ μὲν σφωίτερον γε θεὰρ ἔπος εἰρύσασθαι. ὅσκε θεοῖς ἐπιπείθηται μάλα ἕκλυον αὐλῆ. Relligio nobis vestrum Dea, maxima verbum est. Nam Deus exaudit facilis sua jussa sequentes.
units.tr: Achilles, moreover, added to all these things in Homer: "One must indeed keep in mind the word of the gods; whoever obeys them, they gladly hear him" [Χρὴ μέν σφωίτερον γε θεῶν ἔπος εἰρύσασθαι, ὅς κε θεοῖς ἐπιπείθηται, μάλα τ' ἔκλυον αὐτοῦ]. Reverence for God is for us the greatest word: for God readily hears those who follow his commands.

units.la: Tales olim fuerunt, Scipiones, Fabij, Metelli, Æmylij & alij humano generi Salutares viri: Et fructus diuinitus ce- perunt, meritorum magnitudine, quibus orbem terrarū com- plebant, nominis gloria, qua adhuc florent, dignitate & au- thoritate, qua in vita mirifice fruebantur. Itaq; non illis ub- ique libebat, nec tra Sauromatas & glacialem Oceanum fugere libebat, nec Troglodytarum & Nomadum latebras & recessus expetebant idem; Sed ad consociationem generis humani fouendam, tu- endam & ornandam omne studium, curam, operam & labore conferebant, & Si non respondebatur his ipsorum beneficijs, plus apud se officij residere facilime patiebantur, Et sic ipsis fa- eris declarabant, omni virtute & pietate conjunctionem ge- neris humani custodiendam esse. In hac vero nostra congrega- tione, quae sejuncta est à reliquis hominibus, quorum numerus longe maximus est, qui negligunt Euangelium & Ecclesias, & harum rerum curam se indignam putant, vel propter ventre defendunt usitatos errores, vel delere Ecclesiam conantur: in hoc inquam nostro catu, tanto promtiores & alacriores ad communia vitæ onera adeunda & sustinenda nos esse convenit, quanto majus & certius auxilium nobis diuinitus promissum est & contingit. Nam Spiritus Sanctus petentibus datur, cujus auxilio nihil firmius ac locupletius est. Accedunt & commoda nullis lucris conferenda: Incrementa lucis fidei, exercitia inuocationis, dilectionis & similium virtutum. Quibus in corda sparsis, reuelata facie gloriam Domini intuemur, & in eandem imaginem transformamur tanquam à Domini Spiritu. Neq; desunt fere bona mediocria, quæ vitæ usus postulat, donec Deus nos vacare sua doctrinæ vult, & illa nobis esse, expedire ipsi videtur. Arcani congressus, quales Eleusinia quondam fuerunt, desidiæ ac turpitudinis diuerticula sunt. Scelesti enim oderunt lucem, neq; veniunt in conspectum hominum, ne arguantur; Contra amant honestos congressus boni, qui se Deo ac hominibus probari ac placere norunt. Quamobrem semper in medijs fluctibus gubernationis versati sunt præstantes in Ecclesia viri, & obierunt, quæ jussit pietas, dilectio, honestas, ut docet lux veritatis, vita memoriæ, magistra vitæ, testis temporum, & nuncia vetustatis historia. Horum dissimilimi sunt scurræ velites, qui solent ambulare per tabernas, latitare per popinas, culices pati rotundos, ut ante signanum ipsorum Florum depingit Imperator. Deteriores autem illis sunt homines inquieti, qui non manent intra officij sui metas, & dum regere multa conantur, quæ neq; debent neq; gerere possunt, sibi & Rebuspublicis exitio sunt.
units.tr: Such men once lived: the Scipios, Fabii, Metelli, Aemilii and other men who were beneficial to the human race. They received fruits from God in return for the greatness of their merits, with which they filled the orb of the earth; in the glory of the name by which they still flourish; and in the dignity and authority which they enjoyed wondrously during their lives. Therefore it did not please them to flee to every place, nor to escape to the Sarmatians and the icy ocean, nor did they seek out the hiding-places and retreats of Troglodytes and nomads. Instead, they gave all their zeal, care, effort and labour to fostering, defending and adorning the fellowship of the human race. And if these benefits of theirs were not repaid, they very easily bore that more duty remained with themselves. So they showed by their deeds that the fellowship of the human race must be preserved by all virtue and piety. In this our congregation, which is separated from the rest of mankind, whose number is by far the greatest, and who neglect the Gospel and the Churches, and think themselves unworthy of this care, or who, for the sake of their bellies, defend common errors or try to destroy the Church, in this, I say, our little band, we ought to be all the more prompt and eager to undertake and bear the common burdens of life, as much as the greater and surer help promised and granted us by God is. For the Holy Spirit is given to those who ask, and nothing is firmer or richer than his help. There are also advantages that cannot be compared with any gain: increases of the light of faith, exercises of invocation, love and similar virtues. When these are poured into our hearts, we behold the glory of the Lord with unveiled face and are transformed into the same image, as by the Spirit of the Lord. Nor are the moderate goods that the use of life requires lacking, until God wills us to be free for his teaching, and sees it expedient for us to have them. Secret gatherings, such as the Eleusinian once were, are hiding-places of sloth and baseness. For the wicked hate the light and do not come into the sight of men, lest they be convicted; but good men, who know how to be approved and pleasing to God and men, love honourable gatherings. For this reason outstanding men in the Church have always been engaged in the midst of the waves of government, and have performed what piety, love and honesty demanded, as the light of truth teaches, life of memory, teacher of life, witness of the times, and messenger of antiquity, which is history. Most unlike these are the light-armed buffoons, who are wont to wander through taverns, lurk in eating-houses, and put up with round gnats, as the emperor depicts them before their standard. Worse than these are restless men, who do not stay within the limits of their office, and while they try to manage many things that they neither ought to nor can do, they are a ruin both to themselves and to commonwealths.

units.la: His dicit Poëta:
units.tr: Thus the poet says:

units.la: Crede mihi, bene qui latuit, bene vixit, & intra Fortunam debet quisq; manere suam.
units.tr: Believe me, he who has lived hidden has lived well, and each person should remain within his own fortune.

units.la: Rursus, laudandi non veniunt, qui mediocri industria praediti, rei communi, quæ subinde alumnorum suorum operam exposexposcit, vel non Se offerunt, vel opem negant. Quales fue- runt Ammonius & Euagrius; Quorum alter quasi auribus truncatus, non obtemperabat, vocatus ad gubernationem Ec- clefiæ, cui aptus erat, alter Idoneus ad docendum, quasi lingua excisa esset, ad gloriam Dei illustrandum, donum diuinũ non transferebat. Etsi enim moles negociorum ingens est, &sem- per vires humanæ sunt exiles, & salutaribus actionibus mul- tiplex subinde mora accidit: tamen καδδύναμιν δ' ερδειν ιερ ἀδαναδοιαι Ꝺειοιαι, hoc est, præstare mediocrem scientiam artis, quam facis, & sedulitatem vel Deo satis est. Quare non lan- guescere vel abrumpere bonos conatus & instituta oportet, propter jnuidiam & calumnias maleuolorum, neq; eò, quod nonnunquam, ubi non pepercimus intentioni animi, solicitu- dini, labori, tamen industriam non suffecisse, sed defecisse re- perimus. Homines plæraqz, Solus Deus omnia recte facere po- test. Et quàm sanus fuerit Hippias Eleus, qui se esse omnisci- um professus est, quod solius Dei est, non est obscurum. Certè enim Deus ille non fuit. Solus autem Deus ut omniscius, ita ἀναμάρτητος καὶ ἀνυπεύθυνος est. Quarobrem diuinitatem istam homines æqui, qui seipsos norunt, in alijs non requirunt, Quoniam, ut Lyricus ait, vitijs sine nemo nascitur, optimus il- le est, qui minimis urgetur: Et Stigelius: Non qui multa te- net, sed qui scit idonea vita hic dici sapiens, quo mereatur ha- bet. Sed ad rem præsentem accedo, ne patientia vestra, Re- veredi, amplißimi, ornatißimi & doctißimi viri, abuti videar.
units.tr: Again, those are not to be praised who, though endowed with moderate ability, either do not offer themselves to the common cause, which from time to time calls for the labour of its nurslings, or refuse their help. Such were Ammonius and Euagrius. The one, as if his ears had been cut off, did not obey when he was called to govern the Church, for which he was fit. The other, suited to teaching, as if his tongue had been cut out, did not pass on to the illustration of God's glory the gift he had been given. For although the mass of business is huge, human strength is always slight, and frequent delay attends salutary actions, yet "κατὰ δύναμιν δ᾽ ἔρδειν ἱερὰ ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσι" [to offer sacrifices to the immortal gods according to one's power], that is, to put forward a modest knowledge of the art one practises, together with diligence, is enough even for God. Therefore good endeavours and undertakings ought not to languish or be broken off on account of the envy and slanders of ill-wishers, nor because we sometimes find, when we have spared no effort of mind, anxiety or labour, that our diligence did not suffice but failed. Men for the most part fail; God alone can do all things rightly. And how sound of mind Hippias of Elis was, who professed himself omniscient, which belongs to God alone, is no secret. For that man was certainly not God. God alone, being omniscient, is also "ἀναμάρτητος καὶ ἀνυπεύθυνος" [sinless and unaccountable]. Therefore fair-minded men, who know themselves, do not look for such divinity in others, since, as the lyric poet says, no one is born without faults, and he is best who is troubled by the fewest. And Stigelius says: not he who holds many things, but he who knows how to live well with what is fitting is called wise here, and has what he deserves. But I come to the business at hand, lest I seem to abuse your patience, reverend, most distinguished, most accomplished and most learned gentlemen.

units.la: Præclara res est juuentutis vera institutio, Nam ut germina & flores felices magnum decus addunt & conciliant aruis, & summam spem diuitus ac uberis messis ostendunt: Ita quoq; palàm beatæ sunt Respublicæ, in quibus adolescentia sa- cris & bonis literis imbuitur & excolitur, quæ est magna spes altera, non quidem Romæ vel Troiæ, sed Ecclesiæ, quæ Dei ciui-tas tas est, cuius domesticum inquilinum, verum ac viuŭ membrum esse, summa laus ac felicitas est. Neqz enim hac fidelis & benigna pueritiæ cura aliarum ciuitatum est, quam quæ sunt tabernacula & domus Dei, quæ gloria omnibus victoriis & triumphis, quos miratur mundus, anteferenda est. Sed intelligo quanta diligentia, modestia & patientia ornari docentium munus velit. Et ea est imbecillitas omnium hominum, ut ne minimæ quidem functioni feliciter sustinendæ ullius hominis vires pares sint. Ad hæc infinitæ sunt omnes artes, & crescunt inter tractandum. Itaqz optimus & grauissimus quisqz fatetur, se multa ignorare & multa sibi quotidie esse addiscenda. Denique ignorantia est animi defectus, cui doctrina medetur, quæ ut radices agat in animis, multos annos assiduè repetenda, audienda, dicenda, & ad usum in vita transferenda est, acferè plures sunt, qui ad officium cogendi sunt quam quibus freno opus est. Vbiqz enim experimur, quod Isocrates in suis discipulis sensit. His & aliis multis difficultatibus nostra prouincia dura est. Sed quantæcunqz illæ sunt: tamen hominum candidorum commoditate & studiosa industria atqz obsequio bonorum ingeniorum leniuntur & compensantur, & inuocantibus Deum, auxilium certum venit.
units.tr: The true instruction of youth is a splendid thing. For as buds and flowers add great beauty and favour to the fields and promise a rich and abundant harvest, so commonwealths are plainly blessed in which young people are imbued and trained in sacred and good letters. This is a great second hope, not of Rome or Troy, but of the Church, which is the city of God, and to be its domestic inmate and a true and living member is the highest praise and happiness. Indeed, this faithful and kindly care of childhood belongs to no cities except those which are the tabernacles and houses of God, a glory to be preferred to all the victories and triumphs the world admires. But I understand with how much diligence, modesty and patience the office of teachers must be adorned. And such is the weakness of all men that no one's strength is equal even to the successful discharge of the smallest duty. Moreover, all arts are infinite, and they grow as they are handled. So the best and most serious man confesses that he knows many things not, and must learn many things every day. Finally, ignorance is a defect of the mind, which learning heals; but learning, to take root in minds, must be repeatedly studied, heard, spoken, and carried over into use in life over many years. And there are more who must be driven to their duty than who need a bridle. For everywhere we experience what Isocrates felt with his pupils. Our province is hard because of these and many other difficulties. But however great they are, they are softened and made up for by the kindness of honest men, by the diligent industry and obedience of good minds, and when God is called upon, sure help comes.

units.la: Quare cum diuinitus, ministerio pÿ Magistratus in hoc perantiquo & nobili Emporio gubernationem studiorum huius Scholæ mihi demandari intelligam & agnoscam: eam accipio, non inuitus, ne Deo & honestissimæ Reipublicæ refragari videar; Et principio æternum Deum, pro omnibus beneficiÿs celebro, quibus nobis diuinam bonitatem, & paternam voluntatem assiduè probat, & toto pectore precor, ut per & propter Filium suum, Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, hæc & alia, quæ secundum ipsius voluntatem agimus, gubernet, net, & prosperitate ac successibus donet & ornet; deinde nos collegas adjuuet, una cum discipulis nostris, ut honestate & pietate, doctrina & disciplina partibus nostris rite funga-mur, & hi discendo proficiant ac obaediant. Quamihi mei lo-ci ratio imponit, ea reipsa potius praestare sedulo conabor, quam verbosè polliceri. Quod reliquum est, vobis Reuerendis & amplissimis viris, pietate & doctrinae sinceritate fidis ani-marum Pastoribus, tum strenuis Custodibus disciplinae ac pacis in hac civitate, Dominis, patronis & amicis meis co-lendis, me plurimum debere fateor, quod officij & beneuo-lentiae causa, hac initia vestra, praesentia honestastis, & me meamque operam Scholae, & hanc mihi meaque fidei inpri-mis Commendastis & Commisistis, & qualecunque proami-um audiuistis patienter. Ago reuerenter & studiose gratti-as, & hoc & cetera merita vestra, ubicunque potero, me fideliter memi-nisse declarabo.
units.tr: Therefore, since I understand and acknowledge that by divine providence, through the ministry of the magistrate, the direction of the studies of this school has been entrusted to me in this very ancient and noble trading town, I accept it, not unwillingly, so as not to seem to oppose God and this most honourable commonwealth. And first I praise the eternal God for all the benefits by which he constantly shows us his divine goodness and fatherly will, and with my whole heart I pray that through and for his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, he would govern these and the other things we do according to his will, and grant them prosperity and success, and adorn them. Then I pray that he would help us colleagues, together with our pupils, so that we may duly discharge our parts with honesty and piety, learning and discipline, and that the pupils may progress in learning and be obedient. What my position requires I will strive to perform in deed rather than to promise in words. As for the rest, I confess that I owe very much to you, reverend and most distinguished men, faithful ministers of souls in piety and sincerity of doctrine, and vigilant guardians of discipline and peace in this city, whom I must cherish as my lords, patrons and friends, because out of courtesy and goodwill you have honoured this beginning of ours with your presence, and have commended and committed both me and my work to the school, and especially to my faith, and have patiently heard whatever reward I could offer. I give you thanks reverently and earnestly, and wherever I can I will show that I faithfully remember this and your other services.

units.la: Τέλος καὶ τῷ θεῷ δόξα.
units.tr: The end; and glory to God [Τέλος καὶ τῷ θεῷ δόξα].

units.la: THESES DE PROAERESI HOC EST CONSILIO SEV DELECTU è tertio Ethicorum Aristotelis conscriptæ.
units.tr: THESES ON PROAIRESIS, THAT IS, ON COUNSEL OR CHOICE, drawn from the third book of Aristotle's Ethics.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Consilij ratio, quam Aristoteles Προαίρεσιν dicit, ad omnes virtutes pertinet, è quibus quasuis officia, tanquam ex sacro augustoque fonte manant.
units.tr: The principle of counsel, which Aristotle calls προαίρεσις [proairesis], belongs to all the virtues, and from them all duties flow, as from a sacred and venerable spring.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Quare, quæ Philosophus ea de re tradidit, nos certis capitibus complecti, operæ precium visum est.
units.tr: Therefore it seemed worth our effort to gather into definite chapters what the Philosopher has taught on this subject.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Nam quia delectant omnes bonos, quæ vera sunt, & incipientes, juvare sua studia magnopere cupiunt: hanc operam nemini molestam, discentibus vero non inutilem fore speramus.
units.tr: For since all good people delight in what is true, and beginners above all want to advance their studies, we hope this labour will be unwelcome to no one and not useless to learners.

units.la: IIII.
units.tr: IIII.

units.la: Sequemur autem, quæ autor ille in Analyticis de via definiendi docuit, & in hoc negocio tenuit: nimirum, ea, quæ communia sunt rei propositæ, sumemus & eò usq; persequemur, donec propria efficiantur, quæ in nullam rem transferri possint aliam, cujus præcepti, etiam Cicero in Topicis mentionem facit.
units.tr: We shall follow what that author taught in the Analytics about the method of definition, and kept to in this business: namely, we shall take up what is common to the thing proposed and pursue it until it becomes proper, so that it cannot be transferred to any other thing. Cicero too mentions this rule in the Topics.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Itaq; ut ad rem veniamus: Consilium seu delectum, qui Aristoteli Προαίρεσις est, inter actiones numerari statuimus. Quæ cujusmodi sint, quia multiplices & variæ sunt in præsentia explanandum erit.
units.tr: So, to come to the matter: we hold that counsel, or choice, which for Aristotle is προαίρεσις [proairesis], is to be counted among the actions. Since such actions are many and varied, we must now explain what sort they are.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Nam inquisitioni mentis, ut visioni, rem distantem longiori giori interuallo, admoueri propius oportet. Alioqui non exacte comprehensam, nec satis ab aliis discernat, nec notitiam eius plenam consequatur. Ergo, quæ eminus conspicati sumus, ut contemplemur propius, operam demus.
units.tr: For, just as with sight, a distant object must be brought closer to the inquiring mind, for otherwise the mind will not grasp it exactly, nor distinguish it sufficiently from other things, nor gain a full knowledge of it. So let us take pains to examine closely what we have seen from afar.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Omnia, quæ suscipiuntur ac fiunt, aut sponte suscipiuntur & fiunt, & dicuntur ἐκούσια, vel non sponte, & sunt μὴ ἐκούσια. Quod si ab his, quæ non sponte fiunt, consilium excludatur, de illis, quæ fiunt sponte, id esse relinquetur.
units.tr: Everything that is undertaken and done is either undertaken and done willingly, and is called ἐκούσια [hekousia], or not willingly, and is μὴ ἐκούσια [mē hekousia]. If what is not done willingly is excluded from counsel, then what remains is what is done willingly.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Non autem plures esse formas eorũ,quæ fiunt resipsa docet. Nam cum vel ab externo impulsu, vel ab interna & innata vi, qua aliter agere aut nõ potest aut potest, omnia cieantur, hæc quidem sponte, illa, non sponte fieri dicuntur. In rebus inanimatis & animantibus rationis expertibus, sponte sua idem valet, quod per se, nulla vi coacta aut nulla arte adhibita. In ratione praditis interdum sua vi, per se, non rogata neq; adiuta, interdum etiam sua voluntate.
units.tr: Nor does experience teach that there are more forms of the things that are done. For since all movements arise either from an external impulse or from an inner and innate power, by which a thing can or cannot act otherwise, the former are said to happen willingly and the latter unwillingly. In inanimate things and in animals lacking reason, "willingly" means much the same as "of itself": by its own nature, with no force applied and no art employed. In rational beings, it sometimes means by their own power, of themselves, not asked or helped by anyone, and sometimes also by their own will.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Sed quod inter illa consilium reponi nequeat, videndum est: Quo cognito, facile erit, quod in his recenseatur statuere.
units.tr: But we must consider why counsel cannot be placed among those things. Once this is known, it will be easy to determine what should be counted among them.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Τὰ μὴ ἑκούσια duorum sunt generum: vel ἐξ ἐκούσια vel ἀκούσια. Quorum illa non sponte, hæc invitè suscepta Latinè dici, Dionysio Lambino placet.
units.tr: Things that are μὴ ἐκούσια [mē hekousia] are of two kinds: either ἐξ ἀκουσίων [ex akousiōn] or ἀκούσια [akousia]. Dionysius Lambinus is pleased to call the former things undertaken unwillingly and the latter things undertaken against one's will.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Τὰ μὴ ἑκούσια sunt Aristoteli τὰ δι' ἀγνοιαν καὶ μὴ ἐπίλυπα, quæ per ignorantiam & sine doloris sensu fiunt. τὰ ἀκούσια, τὰ βία, δι' ἀγνοιαν καὶ ἐπίλυπα, id est violenter, per ignorantiam & cum doloris sensu admissa.
units.tr: For Aristotle, the μὴ ἐκούσια [mē hekousia] are τὰ δι' ἀγνοιαν καὶ μὴ ἐπίλυπα [ta di' agnoian kai mē epilypa], things done through ignorance and without any sense of pain. The ἀκούσια [akousia] are τὰ βία, δι' ἀγνοιαν καὶ ἐπίλυπα [ta bia, di' agnoian kai epilypa], that is, things done by force, through ignorance, and with a sense of pain.

units.la: Hæc
units.tr: These

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Hac omnia cum auersari & declinare soleamus, cum eo, quod ad actiones refertur & laudi datur & inter expetenda habetur, consistere poterunt minimè.
units.tr: Since we are accustomed to shun and avoid all these things, they can by no means be reconciled with what is referred to actions, is praised, and is regarded as worth seeking.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Sanè non nisi in scientem atque ex sese agentem & in rebus singularibus occupatum, hoc cadere videtur. Quod si ita se habet, omnino Προαίρεσις est ἐνέργειόν τι, ἓ ἡ ἀρχὴ ἐν αὐτῷ ἐδὸπ τὰ καθ' ἕκαστα, hoc est quiddam sponte susceptum, cujus principium est in ipso cognoscente res singulas, ut e contrario æstimari potest.
units.tr: Clearly, this seems to apply only to someone who knows what he is doing, acts of himself, and is occupied with particular things. If that is so, then προαίρεσις [proairesis] is altogether a certain ἐνέργειά τις [energeia tis], whose origin is ἐν αὐτῷ ἐστι τὰ καθ' ἕκαστα [en autō esti ta kath' hekasta], that is, something undertaken willingly, whose source lies in the one who knows the particular things, as can be judged the other way round.

units.la: XIIII.
units.tr: XIIII.

units.la: Quæ hactenus persecuti sumus, communia quidem ipsa fuerunt alia pluribus, alia paucioribus. At eò usque progressis ubi insistendum est, quasi in justo ad objectum mente Comprahendendum interuallo constitutis, quibus laxa astringantur, promenda & adhibenda sunt. Quo futurum est, ut quod agimus ab aliis distincta τῆς Προαιρέσεως natura appareat & intelligatur.
units.tr: What we have followed so far has been common, some of it shared by many things, some by fewer. But now that we have come to the point where we must stand firm, as if placed at the right distance for the mind to grasp its object, the points that hold the matter together must be brought forward and applied. The result will be that the nature of προαίρεσις [proairesis], which we are discussing, appears and is understood as distinct from other things.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: De præpositis autem, ab humana duntaxat præstantia consilium dependere, intelligi fortassis potuit. Sed oculis & animis ad intuendum & considerandum illud enucleatius exponemus. Nam hac ratione, eò quo tendimus, rectissimè prouehemur.
units.tr: Perhaps it could be understood from what has been said that counsel depends only on human excellence in matters that are preferred. But we shall set this out more fully, so that it can be seen and considered with the eyes and mind. For in this way we shall advance most directly toward where we are heading.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Qua facultate bestias antecellit homo, eius duo membra putantur, ἡ ὀρεκτικὴ καὶ διανοητικὴ. Quibus sectis in minuminutiora paulò, à nonnullis prorsus discrepare, alÿs appropinquare, cum alÿs idem esse, consilium intelligetur. Huc delatis nobis velut in portum optatum, aliquo modo securis in hoc negocio deinceps esse licebit. Quod ut contingat, velis remisque contendamus, commodißimum Ἡης ἀναλύσεως instrumentum ante hac usurpatum resumentes.
units.tr: The faculty by which man surpasses the beasts is thought to have two parts: ἡ ὀρεκτικὴ [hē orektikē], the appetitive, and διανοητικὴ [dianoētikē], the intellectual. If these are divided into smaller parts, counsel will be understood to differ wholly from some, to come close to others, and to be the same as still others. Once we have been brought, as if into a longed-for harbour, we may be somewhat free from worry in this business from then on. So that this may happen, let us strive with sails and oars, taking up again the most convenient instrument of analysis used before.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Quicquid humanarum actionum, vera laudis præconium meretur ac habet, id omne a consilio proficisci, hoc modo ab opinione ipsum distinguens docuit Aristoteles. Quòd cum ita sit, referri ad διανοητικὴν neutiquam poterit.
units.tr: Whatever human actions deserve and possess true praise, Aristotle taught, all proceed from counsel, which he distinguishes in this way from opinion. Since this is so, counsel can by no means be referred to the intellectual part.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Nam cum neque intellectus theoreticus, neque practicus censeri possit, cum suprema hujus facultatis, plures forma non sint, ab hac illud semouere non est operosum.
units.tr: For since counsel can be classed neither as the theoretical nor as the practical intellect, and since the highest forms of this faculty are not many, it is not difficult to separate it from this.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: Principio enim intellectus Theoreticus rebus agentis prorsus non est deditus ac destinatus. Quî jam de eo, a quo semper aliquæ actiones oriuntur, ille dicetur.
units.tr: In the first place, the theoretical intellect is wholly not given over and devoted to acting. How then could that be called the source from which some actions always arise?

units.la: XX.
units.tr: XX.

units.la: Neque item intellectus practicus perhiberi vere potest, cujus imperatis non raro plane contraria a rapidis ac turbulentis affectibus cientur & geruntur. Itaque quàm rectè is actionum fons putetur, nemini potest esse obscurum.
units.tr: Nor can the practical intellect truly be described as this source either, since its commands are often plainly contradicted and overturned by rash and turbulent passions. So how rightly that is regarded as the source of actions can be obscure to no one.

units.la: XXI.
units.tr: XXI.

units.la: Fusius & hac & alia tradidit Aristoteles, quæ nos memores instituti nostri plæraque reliquimus, summe necessaria & rei præsenti accommodata ab eo petentes, & qua potuimus breuitate contexentes. Quapropter ut unde discessimus eò nos recipiamus, perspecto, quod consilium seu Προαίρεσις, διανοητικὴ haberi nequeat, num ὀρεκτικὴ censeri possit, ea, qua capimus ratione videamus.
units.tr: Aristotle treated this and other matters at greater length, but mindful of our purpose we have left out most of them, seeking from him only what is most necessary and suited to the present matter, and weaving it together as briefly as we could. Therefore, so that we may return to where we began, having clearly seen that counsel, or προαίρεσις [proairesis], cannot be held to be intellectual (διανοητικὴ [dianoētikē]), let us see by the method we have adopted whether it can be regarded as appetitive (ὀρεκτικὴ [orektikē]).

units.la: XXII.
units.tr: XXII.

units.la: Diuisa est hæc posterior præstantia humanæ facultas in βούλευσιν & βούλησιν seu in consultationem & voluntatem. Etsi autem sine voluntate consilium non est, tamen vix magis voluntas, quam intellectus practicus asseri id potest, quem à consilio & actionibus ipsum quoque non alienissimum esse constat.
units.tr: This latter excellence of the human faculty is divided into deliberation (βούλευσις) and wish (βούλησις), that is, into consultation and will. Yet although there is no choice without will, it can scarcely be asserted that it is more will than practical intellect, which is clearly not at all alien to choice and to actions.

units.la: XXIII.
units.tr: XXIII.

units.la: Nam velle nos actiones eas, quæ non sunt omnium, aut vires etiam humanas excedunt, nihil prohibet. Sed quod consilium versetur in ÿs, quæ posita in potestate nostra ut plurimum accidunt, exitu & inuento incerto, hoc illud a voluntate non parum dissidere facit.
units.tr: For nothing prevents us from willing actions that are not open to everyone or even exceed human powers. But that choice is concerned with those things which, placed in our power, usually happen with an uncertain outcome and discovery, this makes it differ not a little from will.

units.la: XXIIII.
units.tr: XXIIII.

units.la: Quamobrem aut facultatum hominis insigniorum nullam, aut βούλευσιν id est consultationem esse super est. Quo dato aut posito, adeò nihil sequitur inconueniens, ut nihil magis ad rem dici posse videatur. Nam consilium haud aliter, quàm consultatio cogitatione & ratione utitur, adeoque laudabilia etiam edit opera.
units.tr: Therefore it remains that either none of man's more distinguished faculties is at issue, or it is deliberation (βούλευσις), that is, consultation. Granted or posited this, nothing unfitting follows, so that nothing more suitable to the matter can seem to be said. For choice uses thought and reason in no other way than consultation does, and so it also produces praiseworthy works.

units.la: XXV.
units.tr: XXV.

units.la: Sed tamen προεκλεγλευμένον ti potius, hoc est quiddam de consultatione excerptum & judicio alijs antepositum, quàm βέλευσιν perhiberi Græci vocabuli potestas postulat. Quod paruo discrimine perfectionis scilicet, & temporis a consultatione cum absit, ferè nullius momenti ducitur.
units.tr: But the force of the Greek word requires that it be called something chosen beforehand [προεκλεγμένον], that is, something picked out from deliberation and judged to be preferred to others, rather than deliberation itself. With a small difference of perfection and of time, since it is not absent from consultation, this is held to be of almost no importance.

units.la: XXVI.
units.tr: XXVI.

units.la: Erit igitur Προαίρεσις, ἑκούσιν ti, hoc est quiddam sponte susceptum. Sed non quicquid sponte susceptum est, de eo consilium captum est, verum illud, de quo prius habita deliberatio fuit, quod Græcis προαιρεσὶον est.
units.tr: There will therefore be prohairesis, a voluntary something, that is, something undertaken of one's own accord. But not everything undertaken of one's own accord is that about which deliberation has been taken; rather it is that about which deliberation was held beforehand, which in Greek is προαιρετόν.

units.la: XXVII.
units.tr: XXVII.

units.la: Tale ἑκούσιον cum sit προαίρεσις, ἓς προεκλεγλευμένη vox accedit necessitate quadam, ut emergat definitio, in qua communia rei propositæ usque eò prosecutum esse Aristotelem apparet, dum propria efficerentur, quæ alij nulli adaptata conveniunt, & conjunctim Quadrant. Προαίρεσις ἐστι ἑκούσιον τι προεκλεγλευμένον, ἡ ὄρεξις βουλευτικὴ τῶν ἐφ' ἡμῖν hoc est, delectus vel consilium est quiddam sponte & vero judicio alijs antepositum, vel est appetitio deliberatiua rerum, quæ fieri a nobis possunt.
units.tr: Since prohairesis is such a voluntary thing, the word προεκλεγμένη is added by a certain necessity, so that the definition emerges, in which it appears that Aristotle pursued the common features of the proposed matter so far that his own distinctive features were made, which fit no others; and together they fit exactly. Προαίρεσις ἐστι ἑκούσιόν τι προεκλεγμένον, ἡ ὄρεξις βουλευτικὴ τῶν ἐφ' ἡμῖν: that is, choice or deliberation is something undertaken of one's own accord and chosen beforehand by judgment above others, or it is the deliberative appetite of things which are in our power.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: FINIS.
